title: Why mass resists acceleration
canonical_question: Why does a larger mass need a larger force to reach the same acceleration?
summary: Mass is a measure of how strongly a body resists having its motion changed.
This is about why the relationship exists, not about plugging numbers into a = F / m.

reuse.rationale: Authored fixture node for the E05 registry.

sections.heading: Inertia as reluctance
sections.body_md: Mass is a measure of how strongly a body resists having its motion changed. A more massive body has more of this reluctance, so a given push produces less change. That is the deep reason mass sits where it does in F = ma.

sections.heading: A conceptual, not numerical, point
sections.body_md: This is about why the relationship exists, not about plugging numbers into a = F / m. The larger the mass, the larger the force needed for the same acceleration, because there is more inertia to overcome. Understanding the why makes the formula feel inevitable.

key_points: Mass measures resistance to changing motion.
More mass means less acceleration per unit force.
This explains why mass appears in F = ma.
core.bridge_to_parent: It deepens the meaning of mass rather than computing with it.
